name: Kahlil Gibran
summary: Kahlil Gibran, author of The Prophet, wrote in Arabic and English parables, poems and essays that attacked corrupt clergy, feudal lords and exploitative merchants, called for an awakening of the Middle East, and demanded that husbands treat wives as companions, but he kept out of party politics and left few positions on the questions a quiz asks.

sources.title: Selected shorter works: 'The New Frontier', 'My Countrymen', 'You Have Your Lebanon and I Have My Lebanon' (translations in Terebess Asia Online)
sources.author: Kahlil Gibran
sources.usedFor: Essays on the Middle East's awakening, parasitic politicians, monopolising merchants, corrupt clergy, husbands and wives, and the weakness of his countrymen.

sources.title: Spirits Rebellious (1908; Terebess Asia Online)
sources.author: Kahlil Gibran
sources.usedFor: The narrator's own passage in 'Khalil the Heretic' on rulers, nobles and clergy exploiting the Lebanese farmer.

sources.title: The Garden of the Prophet (1933), 'Pity the nation' passage (Terebess Asia Online)
sources.author: Kahlil Gibran
sources.usedFor: His list of nations to be pitied: bully-hero worship, imported cloth and bread, fragmentation.

sources.title: Khalil Gibran, New World Encyclopedia
sources.author: New World Encyclopedia
sources.usedFor: Biographical outline used to place the works in his life.

booksNotUsed.reason: Read by theme (Marriage, Crime and Punishment, Laws, Freedom, Buying and Selling, Religion): a sermon in the persona of Almustafa, whose images (laws as shadows, freedom as a yoke, marriage with spaces between) do not state a position on any statement.

booksNotUsed.file: 5616 Gibran - The Madman His Parables and Poems.txt
booksNotUsed.reason: Parables told in the voices of characters (the weaver's eye in 'War', the wise king, the good and evil god) that state no position of his own on the statements.
A volume of twenty pencil drawings with an editor's critical introduction on his art; no political statement by him.

booksNotUsed.file: 54580 Gibran - The Forerunner, His Parables and Poems.txt
booksNotUsed.reason: Parables and poems read by theme (kings, slaves, 'War and the Small Nations'); the parables are fables with no stated position on any statement.

notFound.work: Political essays and letters on Syrian and Lebanese independence, the 1916 famine relief and the Pen League (1919-1931), and his Arabic works Broken Wings and A Tear and a Smile as separate texts

tried.where: Terebess Asia Online and the local Project Gutenberg library
tried.how: the translations of the Spirits Rebellious, Broken Wings and Tear and a Smile were read for his own voice; his 1919-20 statements on Syria were not in them
only biographical summaries and the poems turned up, no text of his political statements

notes: First audit. Gibran was a poet and painter who avoided party politics, so his record is words in fiction, parables and a few essays; answers rest on passages in his own voice ('The New Frontier', 'My Countrymen', the narrator's passage in Spirits Rebellious, the 'Pity the nation' passage), with confidence at most medium. Characters' speeches in the stories (the monk's sermon, Farris Effandi, Madame Rose Hanie) were not counted as his. Read and settling no statement: Broken Wings (forced marriage by a bishop's nephew, a novel), A Tear and a Smile, Sand and Foam, The Prophet's chapters, the Madman and Forerunner parables. 'My Countrymen' and 'You Have Your Lebanon' attack servility and foreign tutelage in general terms without stating a position on independence or federation. The New World Encyclopedia entry was read for his life. Not reached: his Arabic letters and the 1919-20 Syrian National Committee statements; most statements are modern and stay null.
